summary: This cycle is emerging from the bottom differently. A holder base that did not capitulate may provide a sturdier foundation, but the early recovery has favored alts, with bitcoin lagging.
body_markdown:
Greg Cipolaro – Head of BitGo Research


## Key Takeaways for Investors


-


The cycle bottomed in July. The drawdown was shallower and shorter than in past cycles, and not all bottom metrics triggered, but we think that is due to a maturation of the asset class, the changing holder base, and more robust industry infrastructure and business practices.


-


Shallowest drawdown on record. Bitcoin fell 54.3% from peak to trough, against 78% to 94% in the prior four cycles. We read this as the profile of a maturing asset.


-


Largest drawdown in dollars. The $1.33T market cap decline exceeded the prior four cycles combined. A smaller percentage move can still put more capital at risk in a bigger market.


-


A bottom without capitulation. Most onchain signals fired at the July 2026 low, but weakly, and realized losses never approached prior panic levels. MVRV never fell below 1.0 and there was no crypto contagion event or mass industry liquidation event.


-


Onchain metrics may be watching a shrinking float. ETFs and corporate treasuries leave little onchain footprint, so the signals that marked four straight bottoms may understate stress.


-


Leverage broke at the top. Open interest collapsed four days after the October 2025 peak and barely moved into the July low. The liquidation that mattered started the drawdown, not marked its end.


-


Lag between a bottom in long-term holders and price was shortened. Accumulation led the price low by 203 days, but the lead time has been highly variable.


-


Dominance is breaking the script. Bitcoin's share of the market normally keeps rising after the price low, but this cycle it has drifted lower. Two prior cycles is a thin sample, so we hold this view loosely.


-


Cycle five is running ahead of schedule. Indexed to each cycle's peak, price is two to three times higher than history at the same point. This is the clearest evidence that this cycle is structurally different.


## The Low Is In, and It Arrived Without a Fight


Bitcoin's cycle low is in. Price bottomed at $57K on July 1, 2026, down 54.3% over 268 days from the October 6, 2025 peak of $126K, and it has recovered substantially since. On paper that looks like every other bear market of the last decade, another gut check for long-term holders. The onchain record says otherwise. This was the shallowest drawdown in bitcoin's history, holders barely flinched, and by most of the metrics that have marked prior bottoms, the market never actually capitulated. In the Sherlock Holmes story behind this note's title, the clue was a dog that did nothing in the night-time, because the dog knew the visitor. Our interpretation is that the cycle repeated, but not all metrics signaled a cycle low. ETFs and corporate treasuries are a growing share of the buyer base, and they leave a much smaller footprint on the indicators that called the last four bottoms. What follows is a review of metrics and our attempt to explain how they may change amidst a changing investor base.


## Looking at the Drawdown Depth and Duration


### Drawdown Was Its Mildest (in Percentages)


Bitcoin fell 54.3% from peak to trough in the current cycle. That is the smallest percentage drawdown in bitcoin’s history. The prior four cycles bottomed at declines of 93.7% in 2011, 87.7% from 2013 to 2015, 84.3% from 2017 to 2018, and 77.6% from 2021 to 2022. Lined up end to end, the sequence reads like a controlled deceleration, 94, 88, 84, 78, and now 54. We think this is what a maturing asset looks like. Deeper pools of capital, more long-term holders, and a market structure built around ETFs, institutional custody, and corporate balance sheets that simply didn't exist for the prior cycles all argue for smaller drawdowns going forward.


### Drawdown Was Its Most Severe (in Dollars)


Bitcoin’s 54.3% drawdown was its shallowest on record by percentage, but the largest in dollar terms. Market capitalization fell $1.33 trillion, from a cycle peak of $2.49 trillion to a trough of $1.16 trillion. That’s more than the prior four cycles’ declines combined: $1.19 trillion. The previous record was $917 billion in 2021–22; 2018’s decline was $266 billion.


Both statements describe the same event because they measure different things. A percentage decline is scaled to the size of the market at its peak, and a dollar decline is not. A market that grew from a $1.2 trillion peak in 2021 to a $2.5 trillion peak in 2025 can shed more absolute capital on a smaller percentage move than a much smaller market ever could on a larger one. Bigger markets lose bigger numbers even when they lose less, proportionally.


Our interpretation is that the maturing-asset story still holds, since drawdowns really have gotten shallower in relative terms. The practical implication is that percentage and dollar measures now tell different stories about risk. The first tells an allocator how much of a position to expect to lose. The second tells you how much capital the market had to absorb to make that happen. A shallower drawdown in a far larger market is still a very large event for the capital actually sitting in the asset.


## What Onhain Metrics Say About the Drawdown


Price alone doesn't tell you whether a drawdown flushed out weak hands or just took the market down without much conviction behind the selling. For that, onchain data is more useful: it tracks what holders actually paid for their coins and whether they're selling at a profit or a loss. Measured this way, July 2026 looks unlike any prior bottom on record.


### The Onchain Scorecard


Before walking through each signal individually, the summary below shows where each one landed at the July 2026 low against where it has typically bottomed in prior cycles. Three of the five did what they have always done at the bottom, just less severely. PSIP fell below 50%, and both LTH-SOPR and aSOPR dipped below 1. The two that did not are the more revealing ones. MVRV never approached the territory that marked every prior low, and realized losses stayed well under the peaks of past cycles. Our interpretation is that the market did bottom, but with far less stress along the way. The sections that follow take each metric in turn and try to explain why.


### MVRV Never Broke Down


Market Value to Realized Value, or MVRV, is the ratio of bitcoin's market capitalization to its realized capitalization. Put simply, it measures what the market is paying today against what the average holder actually paid for their coins and historically it has been one of the best markers of a cycle bottom. A reading below 1.0 means the average holder is sitting on an unrealized loss, and in every one of bitcoin's prior four cycles the bottom arrived with MVRV somewhere between 0.43 and 0.78. At the July 2026 low, MVRV never dropped below roughly 1.10, the average holder stayed in profit through the entire drawdown. That's not what a bottom has looked like before, and of the five onchain signals we track this cycle, MVRV is the only one that never crossed its historical line at all.


### PSIP Crossed Below 50%


Percent of supply in profit, or PSIP, tells the same story from a different angle. It measures the share of all circulating bitcoin currently held at a gain. Prior bottoms clustered near 60% of supply underwater, meaning PSIP fell to roughly 40% at each prior cycle low. This cycle's low pushed PSIP down to about 46% in profit, crossing below the 50% line that has marked every prior cycle's bottom. It's a shallower cross than the roughly 60% underwater levels prior bottoms reached, but it's a cross nonetheless. Unlike MVRV, PSIP behaved the way it always has at bottoms, just less severely.


### LTH-SOPR and aSOPR Both Crossed Below One


The spent output profit ratio, or SOPR, compares the price at which a coin is spent with the price at which it was last moved. A reading above 1 means the average coin changed hands at a profit, and a reading below 1.0 means it changed hands at a loss. aSOPR, the adjusted SOPR, applies the same test to every coin spent on a given day, but it filters out outputs younger than one hour, which strips out the noise from coins shuffled between wallets and not truly sold. LTH-SOPR narrows the lens to long-term holders, the coins that have sat untouched for roughly five months or more, so it tells you what the most patient holders were doing when they finally sold. We use the 30-day moving average for a more clear signal.


Both dipped below 1.0 this cycle, with LTH-SOPR bottoming near 0.85 and aSOPR near 0.98, which confirms that some coins moved at a loss, same as every prior cycle. The depth is where this cycle stands apart. Prior LTH-SOPR troughs ran as low as 0.63 to 0.66, and prior aSOPR troughs sat in the 0.93 to 0.96 range, which makes this cycle's aSOPR low of 0.98 the shallowest dip below 1 in the dataset. Sellers were, on average, closer to breaking even than in any prior downturn, but they were still selling at a loss. This signal fired, it just fired quietly.


### Realized Losses Never Approached Panic Levels


Realized loss is the dollar value lost on coins spent below the price at which they last moved. If a coin last moved at $100,000 and is sold at $60,000, it contributes $40,000 of realized loss. On its own, that number is hard to compare across time, because a loss that was enormous in 2013 is trivial against today's market. We therefore divide it by realized cap, which values every coin at the price it last moved and so approximates what holders collectively paid for the supply. The resulting ratio asks what share of the market's cost basis was surrendered in losses. We use the 14-day average to smooth the daily noise.


That makes it the closest thing onchain data has to a direct read on panic selling, and it was the quietest of the five signals this cycle. The ratio peaked at roughly 0.17%, in February 2026, months before the price low, against 0.22% to 0.91% in the prior four cycles. In no cycle had holders surrendered so little of their cost basis, even at the worst of the drawdown. The metric also never rose into the territory that marked prior lows, and it was already fading by the time price bottomed in July. None of these metrics ever got dark. We think that is the headline and not a footnote. Whatever else happened in July 2026, it was not capitulation in the sense the word has meant for the last fifteen years.


### The Quiet Got Quieter, Just Not Quiet Enough


Realized volatility, the 30-day trailing measure of how much bitcoin's price is actually moving, fell to roughly 43 at the July 2026 low, the lowest trough reading of any cycle in this dataset against prior troughs of 150, 100, 102, and 68. Low realized volatility around a bottom isn't a new pattern. It shows up in every cycle here as sellers exhaust themselves and the order book thins out on both sides. What's different this time is duration. In 2011 and 2015, the window where volatility sat below its own two-year 20th percentile stretched roughly 120 days on either side of the trough. This cycle, that window ran about 49 to 50 days each way, less than half as long. Our interpretation is that the compression regime is real. Bitcoin genuinely got quiet at the bottom, but it resolved faster than history would suggest, consistent with everything else in this report pointing toward a shorter, shallower event rather than a longer, deeper one. The current reading, back up near 49 and sitting almost exactly on its own 20th percentile, suggests the quiet period has already ended rather than still building toward something worse.


### Lead Time Between Long-Term Holders and Price Compressed


Long-term holder supply, defined as coins that haven't moved in over a year, put in a cyclical bottom at 58.4% of circulating supply on December 10, 2025. The price didn't bottom until July 1, 2026, 203 days later. That lag, holders accumulating well ahead of the eventual price low, has shown up in every prior cycle too. It ran 130 days in 2011, 309 from 2013 to 2015, 295 from 2017 to 2018, and 480 from 2021 to 2022. What's notable is the direction. The lead time grew for three straight cycles, from 130 days to nearly a year and a half, before snapping back to 203 days this time. Our best guess as to the reason is that faster price discovery, driven by a broader base of institutional and corporate holders, compressed the whole cycle rather than something specific to holder psychology changing. The practical read for anyone tracking this cohort as a bottom signal is that the signal exists, but the lead time is highly variable.


### The Bottom Was Real, the Capitulation Wasn't


Taken together, four of the five signals point to a bottom. Volatility compressed, long-term holders began re-accumulating before the low, supply in profit fell below 50, and both LTH-SOPR and aSOPR dipped below 1. Those readings were shallower than in prior cycles, but they were there. MVRV is the lone holdout, never falling below 1. A skeptic could call that an unfinished bottom. We think it points to a shallower one: a market that fell 54 and recovered 27 in under three months does not look weighed down by a large supply overhang.


Futures open interest helps explain why. Bitcoin peaked on October 6, 2025. Four days later, open interest fell 19.2%, its largest drop of the cycle, as price took its first real leg down. Leverage broke at the top. By contrast, open interest rebuilt through much of the drawdown and fell only 4.3% into the July 1 low, compared with a 13% drop into the FTX-driven trough in 2022. The sharp flush came in October, not July.


### The Onchain Tape May Be Affected By Changing User Base


There is another explanation worth taking seriously: bitcoin may not have become less risky. Its buyer base may simply have changed. Corporate treasuries, sometimes called digital asset treasuries or DATs, and spot ETFs absorbed a growing share of demand this cycle. Neither leaves the same footprint as an individual trading coins onchain. As the graph below shows, the bitcoin backing ETF shares can remain in custody while those shares change hands. Treasury holdings can likewise stay put until management makes a balance-sheet decision. Stress can build in both vehicles without appearing as coins moving at a loss.


On this reading, cycle five did not break the pattern. Part of the pattern moved outside the onchain indicators’ field of view. Holders may be more patient, while a growing share of trading happens without moving the underlying coins, changing how we read MVRV.


## Where are we Now


### Bitcoin Is Losing Dominance Where It Usually Gains It


Bitcoin's share of the crypto market usually follows a two-part script. A real drawdown hits, alts fall harder than bitcoin, and capital flees back to the pre-eminent asset, dominance rises through the crash and into the early recovery. Later in the cycle, as speculation builds, that flow reverses. Investors swing back out on the risk curve into alts, and bitcoin loses dominance even as its own price marks a new high.


The first half of that script held again this cycle. Dominance rose through every drawdown we have data for: 3.2 percentage points peak-to-trough in 2018, 4.4 in 2022, 5.3 this cycle. The follow graph shows the full picture, bitcoin's share of the market against its own price since 2014, with each cycle's price low marked.


It's the second half that isn't following the script. In both 2018 and 2022, dominance kept climbing after the price low, sometimes with a delay, but climbing (Exhibit 11). This cycle it's doing the opposite: dominance peaked near 69% at the July low and has since drifted down to roughly 67%, alts running harder than bitcoin twelve weeks into the recovery instead of the other way around.


Our read is that this connects to the same shallow-drawdown story running through the rest of this report. The usual early-cycle dominance gain isn't really about bitcoin outperforming on its own merits, it's about a crash forcing investors to re-underwrite the safer asset in the group. This cycle's drawdown, the mildest on record at 54%, may not have been calamitous enough to force that re-underwriting. Without it, the market may be skipping straight to the alt-friendly, later-cycle phase of dominance behavior, without ever passing through the flight-to-bitcoin phase that normally comes first. Two prior cycles is a thin sample for a pattern this specific, so we'd treat it as a plausible read rather than a settled one.


### Cycle Five Is Running Ahead of Schedule


If you index each cycle's price to 100 at its own peak and compare them by days elapsed rather than by calendar date, cycle five is running well ahead of the field. On day 268 after the peak, the day this cycle actually bottomed, the index sat at 48, against 44 in 2013, 33 in 2017, and 35 in 2021. By day 345, the most recent data available, it had climbed to 61, against 32, 20, and 30 for the same day count in the prior three cycles. That isn't a marginal difference. At the same point in the calendar, this cycle is running anywhere from two to three times higher than prior cycles showed. We think this is the single clearest piece of evidence that cycle five is structurally different from what came before it, not just smaller, but faster to find a floor and quicker to leave it.


## Final Thoughts


The byline of this report borrows from Sherlock Holmes, who solved a case by noticing that a dog did not bark during a crime. It stayed quiet because it knew the visitor. We meant the reference to describe the absence of capitulation, but the original logic may be more apt than we intended. The onchain tape may have stayed quiet in July because this cycle's buyers and holders were not the kind of visitors it was built to bark at.


MVRV, SOPR, the share of supply in profit and realized losses were all calibrated on a market dominated by retail wallets, miners and early adopters, a population that sells in size when it is underwater. In prior cycles those holders left clear fingerprints on the way down. This time the stress was far shallower and the duration much shorter.


Our interpretation is that the investor base changed underneath the indicators. US spot ETFs, corporate treasuries and governments now hold a meaningful share of circulating supply, and much of it did not exist at the last trough. These holders rarely move coins onchain the way a retail wallet once did, and when they reduce exposure it often happens through redemptions and balance sheet decisions that cost-basis metrics only partly capture.


On that basis, we believe that the cycle low is in. Long-term holder supply bottomed ahead of price and has been rebuilding, in line with prior cycles, and it fell far less than it did in earlier downturns. Holders were not shaken out like they had in previous cycles, so there was less supply left to change hands at the bottom.


This cycle is emerging from the bottom differently. A holder base that did not capitulate may provide a sturdier foundation, but the early recovery has favored alts, with bitcoin lagging.
